title: Artificial hibernation reveals synaptic engram architecture associated with memory retention.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened all 11 data files from Dryad (CC0, 32.15 MB total): 10 Excel workbooks (Fig1-Fig5, FigS1, FigS6-S8) and FigS2.csv. Counted rows/columns of every sheet with pandas: largest tabular item is FigS2.csv (867,848 rows x 4 columns: running speed in cm/s, treatment, day, animal) from only 3 hibernation animals and 3 controls; next largest is Fig4 sheet E (988 paired correlation values, labelled ShortTerm/LongTerm). Read the full README (file-by-file and variable definitions) off the Dryad landing page and in the downloaded README.md.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The paper itself is paywalled (not in PubMed Central, no open full text), so experimental design details, group sizes per figure and the definition of a 'synaptic cluster' or 'engram synapse' come only from the abstract plus the Dryad README. The 6 MB thermal-camera acquisition software zip (Windows/C++, needs a FLIR C5 camera) was not downloaded or run.

a1_downloadable.note: Dryad deposit is public and CC0; no login or application. The download endpoint is behind an automated bot-check (proof-of-work), which I solved programmatically; a normal browser downloads it directly. All 11 data files retrieved.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. No file contains a prediction target as a column. The interesting target (does a given spine or synapse survive hibernation / is it a clustered engram synapse) is nowhere recorded per item; the files are figure source data where the grouping sits in merged header rows (e.g. Fig1 sheet J puts NoQIH and QIH values in side-by-side unnamed columns) or in a two-row contingency table (FigS7: MSB 4 vs nonMSB 8). Any label would have to be constructed by hand from spreadsheet geometry.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL. There are no features, only the measured outcome itself. The README states plainly that raw two-photon imaging, electrophysiological recordings and electron-microscopy image stacks are excluded for size, so the images and spike trains that would be the model input are absent; what remains is one number per spine, dendrite or image volume plus a condition name.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are documented in the README for every quantity (spine volume um^3, synapse density synapses/um^3, PSD area um^2, firing rate Hz, spatial information bits/spike, velocity cm/s, body temperature degrees C) and match the sheet headers I opened.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL at the biologically meaningful unit. Largest labelled sheet is 988 paired correlation values (Fig4 E); other sheets are 452 morphology values (Fig1 J), 178 place-cell metrics (Fig2 I), 130 spine sizes (Fig3 L), 12-29 electron-microscopy volumes, and 7 dendrites. FigS2.csv has 867,848 rows but they are time bins of running speed from 6 animals, which is 6 independent units, not 867,848.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Whole deposit is 32 MB; every file loaded into pandas in seconds on a laptop.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot check: the Science article is paywalled with no open full text, so the per-figure n values in the paper could not be compared with the sheets. Internal counts are self-consistent (e.g. FigS7 contingency tables sum to the same synapse totals quoted in the README variable list).

a8_label_provenance.note: All values are direct physical measurements (thermal camera, tetrode recordings, two-photon spine volumes, electron-microscopy reconstructions, freezing behaviour scores), not another model's output. Place-cell identity and Bayesian decoding come from the authors' own MATLAB scripts, which are included; that is the only derived quantity.

existing_models.name: SynapseNet (deep-learning tool for automatic synapse segmentation in electron microscopy)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond the bioRxiv abstract seen in search results; reported to segment synaptic vesicles and structures across many electron-microscopy preparations.

existing_models.name: Deep-learning dendritic-spine detection and time-tracking pipelines (e.g. 2D region-based convolutional neural network spine detectors, SpineS longitudinal analysis software)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved; search returned detection/segmentation papers, none predicting which spines survive a perturbation.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is supportable: with at most 988 paired summary values, 7 dendrites and 12-29 electron-microscopy volumes, and with the images and recordings themselves withheld, any model here would be fitting a figure's summary statistics rather than learning biology.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a synapse's shape and neighbourhood to predict whether it survives a hibernation-like shutdown of brain activity.
plain_idea.train_on: Intended input: per-synapse measurements (spine volume, postsynaptic density area, distance to neighbouring synapses, whether its presynaptic partner contacts several spines) from electron microscopy and repeat two-photon imaging. In the deposit only one summary number per item exists, with 130 spines, 452 morphology values and 12-29 image volumes as the largest counts.
plain_idea.predict: Intended output: survives versus eliminated during artificial hibernation (or clustered engram synapse versus other). The truth would come from matching the same spine across imaging days, or from manual electron-microscopy reconstruction of eGRASP-labelled engram synapses; neither matching table is in the files.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Memory researchers argue over whether big stable spines or clustered synapse architecture carries long-term memory; a predictor of which synapses survive would tell them which features to label and image next. As deposited the data cannot test that.

ml_idea: The attractive idea (predict which dendritic spines or synapses survive an activity shutdown, and whether a synapse belongs to a clustered engram, from its morphology and local wiring) cannot be built from this deposit: the per-item features and the survival/engram labels live in the raw two-photon stacks and electron-microscopy volumes, which the README says were deliberately excluded, leaving only figure-level summary values.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not estimated: all 11 files total 32 MB and the 867,848-row CSV loads into pandas in a few seconds using well under 1 GB of memory.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open any figure sheet and ask 'is there one row per spine with both a feature and an outcome?' - the answer is no in all 11 files, and the README confirms the raw imaging and electron-microscopy stacks are not deposited.

verdict_reason: Figure source data only: no per-item features, no label column, and at most 988 summary rows from a handful of animals and 7 dendrites.
